I am unable to proceed. How am I able to resolve this. I have rebooted the miner from the Settings interface but this doesn’t resolve it.

Am I able to go back to the original OS and see if this works?

I look forward to hearing from you

Hello Richard,

Thanks for the photos, they tell me a lot. I opened both. The miner's screen shows HARDWARE PROBLEM with BOARD INITIALIZATION FAILED in blue, and your log shows the real story underneath: probe_regulator(734): TPS546 ID, then board_prepare(881): regulator probe, then TPS546 rail-off command failed and ASIC rails disabled, repeating in a loop. Just above those lines there are also two warnings, gpio: conflict found for GPIO[1] and GPIO[21].

The good news first. The controller side of your Nexus S1 is alive and well. In the same log it connects to solo.atlaspool.io:3333 and parasite.wtf:42069, gets a job and has authorisation accepted. Wifi, the screen, the web interface and the pool side are all working. The only thing failing is the firmware talking to the TPS546 voltage regulator that feeds the hashing chips, which is why it refuses to bring the ASIC rails up and stops at that message. A reboot from Settings will never clear that, because it fails again at the same point on every boot.

Two things cause this pattern, and the GPIO conflicts point at the second one. First, no 12V at the board. The U. lead powers the ESP32 and the display only, so if the 12V supply on the XT30 connector is not actually live, the regulator cannot answer and you get exactly these lines. So please check that the 12V power supply is plugged in at the wall, switched on, and seated firmly at the XT30, and if you have a second 12V supply of the same rating, try it. Second, and more likely given the GPIO warnings, the wrong device profile was picked in the flasher. The Harlo OS flasher asks you to select your model, and the profile tells the firmware where the regulator and the GPIO pins sit. A neighbouring profile loads and boots happily but then fails to find the TPS546, which is what a profile mismatch looks like on screen.

So the fix to try is a clean re-flash with the right profile. Open harlolabs.com in Chrome or Edge on a computer, connect the miner with a USB data cable rather than a charge-only one, and pick the Nexus entry that matches your unit exactly. The supported list names Nexus S1.1, Nexus L1 and Nexus QX1 as separate profiles, so choose the one printed on your board or box and not simply the nearest looking name. Choose the factory image, not the OTA one, and let it erase and install fully. The factory image wipes saved settings, so you will set the wifi and your pool again afterwards, which is fine. Power it up and let the self test run.

On your question about going back to the original firmware, yes, in principle nothing is locked and the flasher erases and writes whatever image you select, so stock can go back on. I would not do that yet though, because the stock image would most likely show you the same failure if the 12V rail is the problem, and it would also hide the log that tells us what is going on. Try the two steps above first.

If it still stops at BOARD INITIALIZATION FAILED after a correct 12V supply and a clean factory flash of the right profile, then we are looking at the regulator itself and I will want a short video of it powering up and a clear photo of the serial number on the unit, and I will take it from there with JD, our hardware lead. I have already passed him what your log shows. The fastest route of all, if you would like a hand while you flash, is our Discord at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf where you can mention @nullhashrate, that is JD, and he is in there most days.

Reply here with what the screen says after the re-flash and we will carry on from there.

Best regards,
Hal, HeliumDeploy technical support

Hello Richard,

That label is the answer, and it is good news for your hardware. I opened it: Model Nexus S1-BTC, power input 12V XT30, serial ending 260040. So you have the original four chip Nexus S1, which runs four BM1373 chips for about 10 TH/s on roughly 150W. The S1-1, also written S1.1, is a different machine: a single one of those same chips, about 5 TH/s on about 75W. Different board, different number of rails, different pin layout.

That explains everything on your screen. You flashed the S1.1 profile onto a four chip S1, so Harlo OS boots happily, brings up wifi, the display and the pool connections, then goes looking for the single chip board's regulator at the address and pins the S1.1 uses. It does not find it, which is the probe_regulator TPS546 ID line, and the two GPIO conflict warnings are the same mismatch showing up on the pin map. It then refuses to energise the ASIC rails and stops, which is the correct and safe thing for it to do. Nothing in that sequence damages the board. Your regulator and your chips are almost certainly untouched, because the firmware never actually powered them up.

So you have not killed the miner. What you have is the wrong hardware profile in flash, and the fix is simply the right image. The catch is that the published Harlo OS model list covers the Nexus S1.1, the Nexus L1 and the Nexus QX1, but not the four chip S1, so there may not be a public S1 profile in the installer yet. That is why nothing you pick in the flasher today will look right to you.

You are correct that going back to stock is the sensible move for now, and yes it is possible. The E.32 is not locked, the flasher erases and writes whatever image you give it, and the stock Nexus S1 factory image will take the board straight back to how it shipped. What I do not want to do is point you at a random file from a forum, so I have asked JD, who builds Harlo OS, for two things: the stock Nexus S1 factory image so you can return to the original firmware, and whether there is an S1 profile, beta or otherwise, for the four chip board. He picks that up Monday from 10am Eastern and the answer comes back to you here.

If you would rather not wait the weekend, the quickest route is our Discord at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf. Post in the Harlo OS channel and mention @nullhashrate, that is JD. He is in there most days including weekends, and this is exactly the kind of thing he answers in a few minutes with the file attached. Until you have the right image, leave the unit unplugged or simply leave it sitting at that message, since it is not trying to drive the chips and cannot come to harm.

Sorry for the detour, and thank you for the clear photos, they made this quick to pin down.

Best regards,
Hal, HeliumDeploy technical support

Hello Richard,

Good news that the original firmware is back on and the miner is running again, and well done for getting there yourself.

On your point about the email, you are right and it is a fair hit. The campaign went to Nexus S1 owners and the flasher only carries a Nexus S1.1 profile, and the two names are close enough that anyone would read them as the same machine. I have put your note in front of the team with exactly that wording, that S1 owners should be told to hold off until there is an S1 profile. They pick it up tomorrow from 10am Eastern. Thank you for taking the trouble to write it up rather than just walking away annoyed, it is the kind of feedback that actually changes a page.

On Harlo Pool, yes, you can mine there on your stock firmware. It is an ordinary stratum pool, so any SHA-256 miner can point at it whatever software it runs. In your stock Nexus interface set the pool to stratum+tcp://pool.harlolabs.com:8888, put your own Bitcoin Cash address in as the worker name, and put x as the password. Your shares count and the block share works the same way. The one part you will not get is the prize spins, because those are tied to Harlo OS reporting in, so with stock firmware you are mining the pool but not spinning the reels.

On the wifi, two things catch most people here. The E.32 in these boards only speaks 2.4 GHz, so if your router broadcasts one combined name for 2.4 and 5 GHz the miner can fail to join it. Splitting the bands, or temporarily giving the 2.4 GHz band its own name, usually fixes it on the spot. The other is the password: avoid special characters where you can, and check there is no trailing space, since the small keyboard on these screens picks them up easily. If the unit has an Ethernet port within reach of your router, a cable sidesteps the whole thing and is the more stable option anyway.

Tell me how the wifi goes when you get to it and I will pick it up from there.

Best regards,
Hal, HeliumDeploy technical support
